CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT / PRIVILEGED

DEAL TEAM REPORT
Change of Control and Assignment Provisions Analysis
Target's Material Contracts — Due Diligence Review
Corporate M&A

Prepared For: Deal Team / Engagement Partners
Prepared By: Corporate M&A Due Diligence Group
Engagement: Analyze Change of Control Provisions Across Target's Material Contracts

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

This report analyzes the change of control ("CoC") and assignment provisions contained in the target company's material contracts reviewed as part of the acquisition due diligence process. The analysis identifies the principal CoC and assignment triggers, consent requirements, acceleration and termination consequences, assignment restrictions, and related provisions across the contract portfolio, and flags material issues requiring deal team attention prior to signing.

Key findings:

1. The target's material contracts contain a range of change of control provisions that will be triggered by the contemplated acquisition. Certain provisions require counterparty consent prior to consummation, whereas others permit automatic termination or acceleration upon a change of control event.

2. The counterparty markup introduces several deviations to the operative agreements which directly affect the scope and consequence of CoC and assignment provisions, including a reduction in the indemnification cap, conversion of the indemnity basket structure, the addition of Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") carve-outs for regulatory action, and a shortening of the survival period for core representations.

3. The disclosure schedules qualify and narrow certain representations that intersect with the CoC and assignment analysis, including two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7 that intersect with the MAE carve-outs proposed in the markup.

4. Per the controlling deal team instruction set forth in the latest partner email, the client will concede the indemnity basket conversion but treats any reduction in the survival period for core representations as a walk-away issue. All analysis herein reflects this controlling instruction.

5. The contemplated acquisition constitutes a "change of control" under substantially all of the target's financing agreements, key customer and supplier contracts, and license agreements. Deal team should prioritize obtaining third-party consents in identified contracts where counterparty consent is required.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
II. SCOPE AND METHODOLOGY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Materials Reviewed

This report is based on the following materials:

• Base deal materials (the operative agreements and related transactional documents) provided in the acquisition data room;
• The counterparty's markup of the operative agreements identifying deviations from firm-standard and market terms;
• Disclosure schedules and exhibits qualifying the base materials (including Schedule 3.7 regarding pending regulatory inquiries, Schedule 5.2 regarding retained liabilities, and Exhibit B setting forth the survival matrix); and
• Deal team correspondence, including the controlling partner instruction on analysis priorities.

B. Definitions

For purposes of this report:

• "Change of Control" or "CoC" means any transaction or event that results in any Person or group, directly or indirectly, acquiring beneficial ownership of more than fifty percent (50%) of the outstanding voting securities or equity interests of the target, or a sale, transfer, or other disposition of all or substantially all of the target's assets.

• "Change of Control Provision" refers to any contractual term that addresses the consequences of a CoC event, including consent rights, termination rights, acceleration provisions, payment obligations, or similar rights of the counterparty.

• "Assignment Provision" refers to any contractual term governing whether, and under what conditions, either party may assign, delegate, or transfer its rights or obligations under the agreement.

• "Material Contract" refers to each contract identified by the target as material to its business in accordance with the disclosure schedules to the operative acquisition documents.

C. Methodology

Each material contract was reviewed for: (i) the definition of "change of control" (if any); (ii) the consequences triggered by a CoC event (consent, termination, acceleration, or other); (iii) consent threshold requirements; (iv) assignment provisions (whether either party may assign without consent, and any permitted-assignee exceptions); (v) notice and timing requirements; (vi) any interplay between CoC provisions and indemnification, representations, and survival provisions; and (vii) any exceptions or carve-out provisions that narrow or expand the effect of CoC or assignment provisions.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
III. KEY PROVISION-BY-PROVISION ANALYSIS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Change of Control Definition

The operative agreements define "change of control" in substantially consistent terms across the material contracts. The common definition captures:

1. Acquisition by any person or group of more than fifty percent (50%) of the outstanding voting power or equity interests of the target;
2. A sale, lease, transfer, or other disposition of all or substantially all of the target's assets;
3. During any period of twelve (12) consecutive months, the cessation of the individuals who constituted the board of directors at the beginning of such period as the majority of the board; and
4. A merger, consolidation, share exchange, or similar transaction resulting in the holders of the target's equity immediately prior to such transaction holding less than a majority of the equity of the surviving entity.

The contemplated acquisition will constitute a change of control under each of these prongs (in particular prongs 1 and 4), meaning that all CoC-triggered provisions in the target's material contracts will be engaged.

B. Consent Requirements on Change of Control

Several of the target's most economically significant contracts require the counterparty's consent or approval before a change of control may occur or take effect. These include:

• The target's primary credit facility and related financing documents, which require lender consent for a change of control (subject to a permitted-acquiror exception in some instances);
• Material customer contracts with the target's three largest customers, each of which contains a change of control consent requirement tied to the customer's perceived relationship and service continuity; and
• IP license agreements (both inbound and outbound), which contain change of control consent provisions that may require renegotiation of royalty terms or license scope.

C. Termination and Acceleration Provisions on Change of Control

Absent obtaining required consent, the following consequences will be triggered by a change of control:

1. Financing Documents: The primary credit facility permits the lenders to (a) declare all outstanding principal and accrued interest immediately due and payable, and (b) terminate all commitments, upon a change of control. This represents a significant liquidity risk if lender consent is not timely obtained.

2. Customer Contracts: The target's largest customer contract contains a change of control provision permitting the customer to terminate without penalty upon a change of control (a so-called "change of control walk" right). This contract represents a significant portion of the target's revenue and is a material deal consideration.

3. IP Licenses: Inbound license agreements contain provisions that terminate or convert to non-exclusive upon a change of control. The conversion or termination of key inbound licenses could impair the target's ability to continue its core operations post-closing.

4. Employment and Retention: Executive employment agreements contain double-trigger change of control provisions that would result in accelerated vesting and severance obligations upon a change of control coupled with termination of employment.

D. Assignment Provisions

1. General Assignment Restrictions: The material contracts reviewed generally prohibit assignment by the target without the prior written consent of the counterparty, subject to limited exceptions permitting assignment to an affiliate or successor-by-merger.

2. Anti-Assignment Effect of Merger or Acquisition: Standard anti-assignment clauses provide that a merger, consolidation, or sale of substantially all assets will be deemed an assignment for which consent is required. As a result, even absent an explicit "change of control" provision, the target's financing documents, customer agreements, and IP licenses subject to anti-assignment covenants will require consent in connection with the contemplated transaction.

3. Permitted Assignees / Exceptions: Certain contracts permit assignment to a wholly owned subsidiary without consent. Others contain a "successor-by-merger" exception. The deal team should confirm the availability of these exceptions on a contract-by-contract basis, as the counterparty's consent may not be required where a permissible assignee is involved.

4. Deal Structure Interactions: The ability to structure the acquisition as a stock purchase rather than an asset purchase, or to assign contracts through a permitted affiliate entity, may affect which consent requirements are triggered. The deal team should coordinate with tax and structuring advisors on this point.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
IV. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP DEVIATIONS AND THEIR IMPACT ON COC AND ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The counterparty's markup of the operative agreements introduces several deviations from the firm-standard base materials. These deviations directly bear on change of control and assignment analysis and must be addressed:

A. Indemnification Cap Reduction

The counterparty's markup silently reduces the indemnification cap as compared to the base agreement. The reduced cap directly affects the risk allocation post-closing in respect of breaches of representations, warranties, and covenants that may relate to CoC or assignment matters. In particular, a reduction in the cap limits the buyer's recourse for unconsented change of control issues that may surface post-closing.

DEAL TEAM RECOMMENDATION: Flag the cap reduction. Evaluate whether the reduced cap is consistent with market practice for a transaction of this size and risk profile. If the reduction is material, push back or seek compensating protections.

B. Basket Conversion (Deductible to Tipping Basket)

The counterparty's markup converts the indemnity basket from a deductible (i.e., the buyer bears the first dollar of losses up to the basket threshold) to a tipping basket (i.e., once the basket threshold is reached, the buyer may recover all losses including those below the threshold).

Per the controlling deal team instruction (latest partner email), the client will concede the basket conversion. No further negotiation is required on this point.

C. MAE Carve-Outs for Regulatory Action

The counterparty's markup adds carve-outs to the definition of "Material Adverse Effect" for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter. Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect directly with these proposed carve-outs.

The significance of this deviation for CoC/assignment analysis is that the MAE carve-outs narrow the conditions to closing and the seller's exposure for regulatory-driven deterioration that may be triggered by, or develop following, the change of control event. The two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7 heighten this risk — if the MAE carve-outs are accepted without limitation, the buyer would bear the risk of any adverse regulatory outcomes arising from these inquiries.

DEAL TEAM RECOMMENDATION: These MAE carve-outs must be carefully reviewed. The counterparty should be required to either (i) limit the carve-out to regulatory actions of which it has no knowledge, or (ii) provide a specific, negotiated exception for the two disclosed pending regulatory inquiries.

D. Survival Period Reduction (WALK-AWAY ISSUE)

The counterparty's markup shortens the survival period for the core representations set forth in the agreement. Specifically, the markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core reps. This conflicts directly with Exhibit B, which sets forth the survival matrix in the base materials.

Per the controlling deal team instruction (latest partner email), the client treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. The deal team should treat this as a non-negotiable term. Any proposed reduction in the survival period for core representations should be rejected outright.

DEAL TEAM RECOMMENDATION: Reject the survival period reduction. The survival matrix in Exhibit B represents the firm's minimum acceptable position, and any reduction is a deal-breaker per the controlling client instruction.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
V. SCHEDULE-BY-SCHEDULE RECONCILIATION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Schedule 3.7 — Pending Regulatory Inquiries

Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect with the MAE carve-outs in the counterparty's markup. These inquiries must be factored into the risk profile:

• Non-disclosure of the inquiries in Schedule 3.7 would have rendered the counterparty's MAE carve-outs broader than warranted by disclosure;
• The carve-outs, if not capped, could excuse performance based on adverse outcomes of these disclosed inquiries without allocating risk appropriately.

The deal team should require that Schedule 3.7 disclosures be deemed incorporated into the MAE carve-out analysis, and that either (i) the carve-outs be narrowed or (ii) the buyer receive indemnification protection for any MAE attributable to the disclosed inquiries.

B. Schedule 5.2 — Retained Liabilities

Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. The basket conversion (conceded) and the cap reduction (to be addressed) interact with Schedule 5.2. Any retained liabilities that fall within the reduced indemnity cap would have materially reduced recovery as compared to the base agreement.

C. Exhibit B — Survival Matrix

Exhibit B sets the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change contradicts. Per the controlling instruction, this is a walk-away issue and must be preserved in its original form.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
VI. CHANGE OF CONTROL CONTRACT-BY-CONTRACT SUMMARY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Below is a summary of CoC and assignment provisions by contract category:

[Contract Type]           [CoC Trigger]          [Consent Required?]            [Consequence on CoC]

Credit Facility           Yes (50%+)             Yes (lender consent)           Acceleration & termination of commitments

Largest Customer          Yes (50%+)             Yes (customer consent)         Termination right (customer "walk" right)

Inbound IP Licenses       Yes (50%+)             Consent not explicit; deemed  Termination / conversion to non-exclusive
                                                 assignment applies on merger

Outbound IP Licenses      Limited (asset sale)   Yes (licensor consent)         Termination

Supply Agreements         Yes (50%+)             Varies by counterparty         Repricing/termination

Executive Employment      Yes (50%+, double      N/A                            Accelerated vesting; severance
Agreements                trigger)

Equipment Leases          Yes (50%+)             Lessor consent                 Termination; early termination fees

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
VII. KEY ISSUES FOR DEAL TEAM ATTENTION
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. CONSENT STRATEGY: Develop a comprehensive consent strategy for contracts requiring counterparty consent on change of control. Prioritize the credit facility, top customer contracts, and inbound IP licenses. Consider whether the consent requests should be made pre-signing or post-signing.

2. SURVIVAL PERIOD (WALK-AWAY): Reject the counterparty's attempt to shorten survival of core representations. Preserve Exhibit B as agreed. Treat as non-negotiable per the controlling client instruction.

3. BASKET CONVERSION (CONCEDED): The client has authorized concession of the deductible-to-tipping basket conversion. No further negotiation required.

4. MAE CARVE-OUTS: Negotiate narrow carve-outs for regulatory action that do not excuse performance attributable to the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7. Require disclosure-specific carve-outs.

5. INDEMNIFICATION CAP: Evaluate the reduced cap against market norms. If below market, push back or seek other compensating protections (e.g., additional survival, broader fraud exception).

6. SCHEDULE RECONCILIATION: Ensure the schedules (3.7, 5.2, and Exhibit B) are fully reconciled with both the base agreements and the counterparty markup prior to execution. Confirm that no scheduled exception has been silently overridden.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
VIII. RECOMMENDED NEXT STEPS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Compile a complete inventory of affected material contracts requiring counterparty consent, with contract-by-contract notice dates and consent deadlines.

2. Prepare consent request letters for priority contracts, including the credit facility and top customer contracts.

3. Negotiate the MAE carve-out provisions with the counterparty, ensuring the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7 are excluded from any broad carve-out.

4. Reject the survival-period reduction for core representations in accordance with the controlling client instruction. Preserve Exhibit B in full.

5. Concede the basket conversion as authorized by the deal team instruction.

6. Re-evaluate the indemnification cap reduction in light of (i) the conceded basket conversion and (ii) the required survival period, to ensure the overall package is acceptable to the client's risk tolerance.

7. Coordinate with tax and structuring advisors to determine whether the acquisition structure (stock vs. asset) affects which assignment restrictions and consent requirements will be triggered.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DISCLAIMER

This report is prepared for the exclusive use of the deal team and the engagement partners in connection with the contemplated acquisition. It constitutes privileged attorney work product and confidential client communications. This report is not a legal opinion and should not be relied upon as such. Counsel should be consulted before acting on any recommendation herein.

END OF REPORT
